notes.meaning: Moses looks back across Israel's history and declares that God has always been the true home and shelter for His people. Even when Abraham's family and the Israelites in the desert lived in tents without a permanent country, they were secure in God's care. Believers in every age find their lasting safety in the Lord Himself rather than in worldly kingdoms.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars question Moses' authorship, suggesting the title represents a later tradition and dating the psalm to the Babylonian exile or a later period.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine suggested that 'generations' may refer to two groups: the Old Covenant under Moses and the New Covenant he foretold.

notes.meaning: Before any part of the created world was made, God existed without beginning. Mountains appear ancient and permanent to human eyes, but God brought them into being like a birth. Because God has always been God and never ends, mortal people can safely trust Him as their everlasting refuge.

God holds absolute authority over human life and commands dying humanity to return to the dust. This echoes the sentence spoken after the fall of man in the Garden of Eden. Just as a potter can break a clay vessel, God brings earthly life to an end with a word, yet He also holds the power to call the dead back to life in the resurrection.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Following the Latin text, Augustine read this verse as a prayer asking God not to let humans turn downward toward earthly cravings.

notes.meaning: Time looks entirely different to an eternal God than it does to mortal human beings. Even a thousand years feels no longer to Him than a single day that is already over, or a short night watch spent sleeping. Because time cannot limit God, believers should not measure His promises by their own fleeting lifespans.

Human life passes quickly and without warning, like people swept away by a sudden flash flood. We are like wild grass that springs up fresh and green at sunrise, only to be cut down and withered before the sun sets. Life is fragile and brief, and death can bring it to an end at any moment.

Human frailty and death are not mere natural accidents, but the result of God's holy displeasure against sin. The Israelites felt this deeply in the wilderness, where a whole rebellious generation died before entering the promised land. A true sense of God's judgment leads His people to humble themselves in holy fear.

Nothing can be hidden from God, because He sets both open rebellions and hidden thoughts directly before His face. Even sins committed in total darkness are plainly seen under the bright light of His holy presence. Since God overlooks nothing, sinners cannot cover their guilt or make excuses before Him.

A life spent under God's displeasure drains away in sorrow, like a generation wandering in the wilderness. Our earthly years vanish quickly like a spoken story, a fleeting thought, or a dying sigh. Sin makes life feel empty and brief when it is lived apart from God's favor.

A normal human life lasts about seventy years, or eighty for those with greater bodily strength. Even the proudest years and highest achievements of old age are often accompanied by pain, hard labor, and failing health. Life rushes by swiftly like a bird taking flight, and then the soul passes into eternity.

No human being can fully measure or comprehend how great God's holy anger against sin truly is. The fear and reverence God deserves is fully matched by the reality of His righteous judgment. Very few people take this seriously enough to turn from sin while they have the chance.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine viewed earthly troubles as God's mercy to turn sinners away from eternal punishment, warning that leaving a sinner undisciplined in this life can be a heavier form of anger.

notes.meaning: We must ask God Himself to teach us to recognize how short and fragile our earthly lives really are. Numbering our days does not mean trying to predict the future, but living each day with eternity in view. Honest reflection on our mortality leads to a truly wise heart that seeks God and turns away from foolish choices.

Moses pleads with the Lord to turn away His anger and show mercy to His suffering people. The cry 'how long?' expresses deep sorrow while longing for God's favor to return. Asking God to relent does not mean He changes His mind like a human, but that He will change His dealings from judgment to compassion.

True satisfaction and lasting peace can only be found in God's faithful love, not in earthly things. The psalmist asks for this mercy to arrive quickly, like the dawn breaking after a dark night of sorrow. When believers are filled with God's loving favor, they can rejoice through all the days they have left.

The prayer asks God to balance out their past hardships with an equal measure of joy and blessing. Israel had spent forty long years suffering under chastisement in the desert, and they asked for a restoration that would heal that pain. Believers can confidently ask God to give them spiritual joy that matches the depth of their troubles.

The people pray to see God's powerful acts of salvation and care on display during their lives. Even though the older generation had to die in the desert, they pleaded that their children would see God's glorious promises fulfilled. Believers find comfort when they know that the next generation will see the Lord's power and honor Him.

The psalm closes with a plea for God's gracious favor and beauty to rest upon His people. Human work has no lasting value unless God blesses it and gives it permanent success. By repeating the request, the psalmist earnestly asks that God will make their daily efforts and holy service endure long after they are gone.
